blocks.text: The cerebrum has four major lobes (frontal, temporal, parietal and occipital). The lobar surface is heavily folded into sulci (valleys) and gyri (ridges); primary (major) sulci are more invariant in appearance than secondary (minor) sulci.

blocks.title: Major sulci/gyri and the function the notes assign to each
rows: Divides frontal lobe from parietal lobe
Divides frontal lobe from temporal lobe
Deep in the Sylvian fissure; sometimes regarded as the fifth lobe
Middle frontal gyrus (between superior and inferior frontal sulci)
Anterior cingulate gyrus (adjoining the cingulate sulcus, medial frontal lobe)
Inferior parietal lobe (angular and supramarginal gyri; interparietal sulcus separates superior and inferior parietal lobes)

blocks.text: The lateral sulcus (Sylvian fissure) is what divides the frontal lobe from the temporal lobe - the central sulcus is the tempting distractor (it divides frontal from parietal). The explanation adds that the lateral sulcus divides the frontal **AND** parietal lobes from the temporal lobe.

Primary sensory cortex = postcentral gyrus (Brodmann areas 3, 1, 2); the precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex) is the distractor offered beside it. Lesions of the primary somatosensory cortex give agraphesthesia, astereognosis, and loss of vibration, proprioception and fine touch.

Motor cortex = precentral gyrus (Brodmann area 4, Penfield's homunculus); the supplementary motor area (area 6) lies immediately anterior to the motor strip, and the postcentral gyrus is the distractor.
Taste sensation is served by the anterior insula (with the frontal operculum on the inferior frontal gyrus) - amygdala, hippocampus, prefrontal cortex and entorhinal cortex are the distractors.

blocks.subtopic: Angular gyrus, arithmetic and Gerstmann syndrome
blocks.note: Notes only say the inferior parietal lobe (angular and supramarginal gyri) is important for visuospatial attention. **Q3** explanation adds: angular gyrus = normal arithmetical ability; Gerstmann syndrome = acalculia, finger agnosia, left/right confusion and agraphia, attributed to a lesion of the angular gyrus of the dominant parietal lobe. Not covered in the notes.

blocks.text: Nominal aphasia (cannot name objects despite plenty of words, can usually copy written material) localises to the angular gyrus - not Broca area or the inferior frontal gyrus, which are among the distractors.

blocks.subtopic: Angular gyrus and language / nominal aphasia
blocks.note: **Q25** explanation: angular gyrus (Brodmann area 39) is involved in processing auditory and visual input and language comprehension; lesions are associated with anomia. **Q24** localises nominal aphasia to the angular gyrus. The notes do not state this.

blocks.subtopic: Prefrontal cortex: maturation and size
blocks.note: **Q13** explanation: the prefrontal cortex is one of the last brain regions to mature, with lesions producing disinhibition, apathy, loss of initiative and personality change. **Q43** explanation: it occupies nearly ==30%== of the brain. Neither is in the notes.

blocks.text: The prefrontal cortex is the last brain region to mature (amygdala, midbrain, parahippocampal cortex and thalamus are the distractors); its lesions present with disinhibition, apathy, loss of initiative and personality change.

blocks.subtopic: Frontal lobe damage: forced utilisation and personality change
blocks.note: **Q19** explanation: damage to the orbitofrontal region can give forced utilisation behaviour. **Q34** (personality change, disinhibition, poor judgement, irritability) is answered frontal lobe. **Q31**: orbitofrontal cortex has a prominent role in social valuation and damage can cause a pseudopsychopathic syndrome. The notes only give orbitofrontal = associative learning and decision-making.

blocks.text: 'Social valuation' = orbitofrontal cortex; the explanation says other regions (temporoparietal junction, anterior cingulate cortex, fusiform gyrus) also play a part, but anterior cingulate gyrus is the distractor here. Damage to the orbitofrontal cortex can cause a pseudopsychopathic syndrome.

A vignette of personality change, social disinhibition, poor judgement and irritability points to the frontal lobe (explanation: apathetic indifference that can suddenly explode into impulsive disinhibition) - not temporal or parietal lobe.

blocks.subtopic: Temporal lobe aura and mirror neurons
blocks.note: **Q22** explanation: epileptic aura arises from a circumscribed part of the temporal lobe (e.g. olfactory aura from the uncus). **Q52**: mirror neurons are in the inferior frontal (and superior parietal) cortex. Neither is in the notes.

blocks.subtopic: Cerebral blood flow and hallucinations/delusions
blocks.note: Mock explanation (keyed: left medial temporal cortex): patients with schizophrenia and frequent auditory hallucinations show reduced grey matter density and neuronal activation; functional magnetic resonance imaging shows reduced activation in the left temporal lobe and anterior cingulate cortex, and the abnormalities converge in the superior gyrus of the left temporal lobe. The distractors include the right medial temporal cortex, caudate nucleus and prefrontal cortex. Not in the notes.

items.text: The prefrontal cortex occupies nearly ==30%== of the brain (20, 70, 50 and 10 are the other options).
The last part of the brain to mature is the anterior frontal pole (pre-frontal cortex); the frontal lobe is the last area to develop and development continues into the twenties.
Forced utilisation behaviour = frontal lobe (orbitofrontal) damage: the patient picks up and uses objects placed in front of them even when told not to.
Epileptic aura = temporal lobe; the olfactory aura arises from the uncus (medial-inferior surface of the temporal lobe).

Disgust: functional imaging shows consistent change in the anterior insular region (supplementary motor area, dorsomedial thalamus, posterior hippocampus and anterior cingulate cortex are the distractors).

Disengagement of attention is mediated by the medial parietal cortex - the explanation notes it is affected early in Alzheimer disease, with attentional deficits before language and visuospatial deficits.

Mirror neurons are in the inferior frontal (and superior parietal) cortex, active both when performing and when observing an action - the inferior parietal lobe and lateral frontal cortex are near-miss distractors.
The temporal lobe is the lobe first affected in Alzheimer disease (via the entorhinal cortex) - prefrontal, frontal, parietal and occipital lobes are the distractors.

bullets.text: Four lobes (frontal, temporal, parietal, occipital); folded into sulci (valleys) and gyri (ridges).
Central sulcus divides frontal from parietal lobe; lateral (Sylvian) sulcus divides frontal from temporal lobe; insula (deep in the Sylvian fissure) = primary gustatory cortex.
Precentral gyrus (frontal) = primary motor cortex; postcentral gyrus (parietal) = primary somatosensory cortex; both with a homunculus.
Middle frontal gyrus = dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (executive function); anterior cingulate = motivation; orbitofrontal cortex = associative learning and decision-making.

Superior temporal gyrus = primary auditory cortex; calcarine sulcus (medial occipital) = primary visual (striate) cortex; inferior parietal lobe (angular + supramarginal gyri) = visuospatial attention.
Lateral sulcus (Sylvian fissure) divides frontal and parietal lobes from the temporal lobe; the central sulcus is the distractor.
Taste: primary gustatory cortex = anterior insula plus frontal operculum.
Prefrontal cortex is the last region to mature; lesions give disinhibition, apathy, loss of initiative, personality change.

blocks.text: Most fundamental brain functions are represented bilaterally; higher associative functions usually lateralise to one hemisphere. Language comprehension is localised to the left temporal cortex while prosody (tonal modulation of speech) seems limited to the right hemisphere.

The hemisphere contralateral to the dominant hand is the dominant hemisphere and mediates language and speech functions. Dominance can be tested with Annette's handedness scale or the Edinburgh handedness inventory, but handedness is not always the same as dominance.

blocks.title: Hemisphere dominance by handedness (as stated in the notes)

blocks.text: Dominance question: 'Most left-handed individuals have left cerebral dominance' is the true statement; 'right-handed individuals **ALWAYS** have right...' is an absolute-language distractor. Explanation figures: ==90%== right-handed, ==99%== of right-handers left-dominant, ==67%== of left-handers left-dominant (the other ==33%== mixed or right) - this differs from the notes' ==64%== left / ==20%== right / ==16%== bilateral.

blocks.subtopic: Left-handers and left language dominance: figures differ between notes and bank
blocks.note: Notes (p3) give ==64%== left / ~==20%== right / ==16%== bilateral for left-handers. **Q50** (and **Q8**) explanation states ==90%== of people are right-handed, ==99%== of right-handers have left-hemisphere language dominance, and of the ==10%== left-handers ==67%== have left-hemispheric language dominance (==33%== mixed or right). **Q50**'s keyed answer is 67; **Q8**'s keyed answer is 'most left handed individuals have left cerebral dominance'. Be aware of both figures. NEEDS VERIFICATION: the notes also say ==10%== of right-handers are right-hemisphere dominant (page 3), but the same **Q50**/**Q8** explanation says ==99%== of right-handers have left-hemisphere language dominance, which leaves only about ==1%== right-dominant. Check which figure the exam expects.

blocks.text: Size asymmetry: the planum temporale is a triangular region on the upper surface of the superior temporal gyrus, important for language processing, and larger on the left than the right hemisphere in ==65%== of brains. It is probably the most asymmetrical structure in the human brain, some individuals having a five times larger planum temporale on the left. This asymmetry is reportedly reduced or reversed (right>left) in schizophrenia.

In healthy right-handed people it is Heschl's gyrus (primary auditory cortex) as well as the planum temporale that is larger on the left - frontal lobe, hippocampus, inferior temporal gyrus and caudate are the distractors.

blocks.caption: Table: Left Hemisphere lesions vs Right Hemisphere lesions. Left: Aphasia; Right-left disorientation; Finger agnosia; Dysgraphia (aphasic); Dyscalculia (number alexia); Limb apraxia. Right: Visuospatial deficits; Anosognosia; Neglect; Dysgraphia (spatial, neglect); Dyscalculia (spatial); Constructional apraxia, Dressing apraxia. Bottom row spanning both columns: Face recognition (bilateral).

blocks.title: Effects of left vs right hemisphere lesions (lists as printed in the notes)

blocks.text: Left-hemisphere lesion effect keyed as alexia with agraphia (acquired dyslexia with right-sided motor deficits) - even though 'apraxia' is also an option and the notes list limb apraxia under left lesions, so the bank answer is not in the notes' left-lesion list.
Face recognition is listed in the same table as bilateral.

Face recognition: the fusiform gyrus (temporal lobe), which causes prosopagnosia when damaged bilaterally - amygdala, nucleus accumbens, prefrontal cortex and left inferior frontal area are the distractors.

blocks.subtopic: Alexia with agraphia (Q7) and non-dominant hemisphere function (Q29)
blocks.note: **Q7** (left hemisphere lesion effect) is keyed 'alexia with agraphia': explanation says dominant (usually left) hemisphere lesions impair reading (acquired dyslexia), with right-sided motor deficits and agraphia. The notes' left-lesion list does not contain this. **Q29** is keyed 'pictorial memory' as a key function of the non-dominant hemisphere (picture memory predominantly affected by right brain injury) - also not in the notes.

blocks.text: Key function of the non-dominant hemisphere = pictorial memory (picture memory predominantly affected by right brain injury; verbal memory by left); logical reasoning, analytical capacity, verbal learning and language are the dominant-hemisphere distractors. The explanation notes this is disputed.

bullets.text: Fundamental functions are bilateral; higher associative functions lateralise (language comprehension: left temporal; prosody: right).
Dominant hemisphere = contralateral to the dominant hand and mediates language/speech; tested by Annette's scale or Edinburgh inventory; handedness is not always dominance.
Right-handers: left dominant mostly, 10% right dominant (NEEDS VERIFICATION: question bank implies about 1%). Left-handers: 20% right, 64% left, 16% bilateral (Q50 explanation gives 67% left).
Planum temporale: larger on the left in 65% of brains, most asymmetrical structure; reduced or reversed in schizophrenia.

Left lesions: aphasia, right-left disorientation, finger agnosia, aphasic dysgraphia, number-alexia dyscalculia, limb apraxia. Right lesions: visuospatial deficits, anosognosia, neglect, spatial dysgraphia/dyscalculia, constructional and dressing apraxia.
Left-handers: bank explanation gives 67% left-hemisphere language dominance (notes: 64%).
Left > right asymmetry in right-handers: planum temporale AND Heschl's gyrus.
Face recognition = fusiform gyrus; bilateral damage gives prosopagnosia.

facts.label: Left-handers with right / left / bilateral dominance

sections.title: 3. Limbic system, Papez circuit and medial temporal structures

blocks.text: Broca first described the limbic lobe. Papez and later Maclean assigned the function of emotional processing to limbic structures, though this view is challenged in recent times.

Hippocampus is the Papez-circuit answer; temporal pole, medullary centre, trapezoid body and red nucleus are the distractors. Papez circuit per the explanation: hippocampus, fornix, mammillary bodies, anterior thalamic nucleus, cingulate gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus.

**NOT** part of the Papez circuit: Heschl's gyrus (mammillary body, parahippocampal gyrus, cingulate gyrus and hippocampus are). The explanation adds that the limbic boundaries were later expanded to include amygdala, septum, basal forebrain, nucleus accumbens and orbitofrontal cortex.

blocks.forTopic: Papez circuit core structures in order
blocks.mnemonic: Hungry Frogs Munch Ants, Chewing Pebbles

blocks.text: The boundaries of the limbic system were subsequently expanded beyond the Papez circuit to include the amygdala, septum, basal forebrain, nucleus accumbens and orbitofrontal cortex.

The limbic system is thought to mediate emotional responses (through the amygdala), influence neuroendocrine responses (via the hypothalamus) and regulate the reward system (via the nucleus accumbens). It is often considered evolutionarily older than the higher cortical centres.

blocks.title: Medial temporal structures
rows: Include the hippocampus, amygdala, entorhinal and parahippocampal cortex
Important role in memory processes; one of the few brain regions with continuous production of new neurons in adult life
Crucial for fear conditioning and emotional regulation

blocks.text: Amygdala '**NOT** correct' statement = 'learning does not occur without amygdala-mediated consolidation' (absolute-style distractor): learning and consolidation can occur despite amygdalar damage, especially without emotional valence; damage does cause loss of fear conditioning and, in monkeys, loss of maternal behaviour.

blocks.subtopic: Kluver-Bucy syndrome
blocks.note: Mock explanation (keyed: amygdala): the syndrome results from temporal lobe lesions involving parts of the amygdala; lesions of the hypothalamus, cingulate cortex or septal area do not produce it. Distractors: medial dorsal thalamus, lateral hypothalamus, globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus. Not in the notes.

blocks.subtopic: Dentate gyrus, entorhinal cortex and hippocampal blood supply
blocks.note: **Q17** (answer hippocampus): the dentate gyrus is the input region of the hippocampus and one of the few regions showing adult neurogenesis. **Q20**/**Q54** (answer temporal lobe / entorhinal cortex): the entorhinal cortex is one of the earliest regions affected in Alzheimer disease. **Q48**/**Q45**: the hippocampus (dentate gyrus) is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery (with the anterior choroidal artery). The notes mention the entorhinal cortex and hippocampal neurogenesis only in the Papez/medial temporal context.

blocks.text: The dentate gyrus is in the hippocampus (not hypothalamus, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, amygdala or red nucleus); it is the hippocampal input region and one of the few regions with adult neurogenesis.

Early Alzheimer disease: prominent change in the entorhinal cortex (main input to, and target of, the hippocampus; one of the earliest affected regions) - prefrontal cortex, superior temporal gyrus and caudate are the distractors.
Hippocampus blood supply = posterior cerebral artery (with the anterior choroidal artery) - not the middle or anterior cerebral artery or posterior inferior cerebellar artery.
Posterior cerebral artery occlusion affects the dentate gyrus (hippocampus) - cingulate gyrus, corpus callosum, uncinate gyrus and arcuate fasciculus are the distractors.

bullets.text: Papez circuit: hippocampus > fornix > mammillary bodies > mammillothalamic tract > anterior thalamic nucleus > genu of internal capsule > cingulate gyrus > parahippocampal gyrus > entorhinal cortex > perforant pathway > hippocampus.
Limbic boundaries expanded to amygdala, septum, basal forebrain, nucleus accumbens, orbitofrontal cortex.
Limbic roles: emotion (amygdala), neuroendocrine (hypothalamus), reward (nucleus accumbens); evolutionarily older than higher cortex.
Medial temporal structures: hippocampus, amygdala, entorhinal and parahippocampal cortex.
Hippocampus: memory; continuous adult neurogenesis. Amygdala: fear conditioning and emotional regulation.
Heschl's gyrus is NOT in the Papez circuit.
Early Alzheimer disease: entorhinal cortex is one of the earliest affected regions.
Kluver-Bucy syndrome = amygdala (temporal lobe) lesions (not in notes).

blocks.text: The basal ganglia are gray matter nuclei forming the largest subcortical structure in the brain. They are involved in planning and programming of movement and have a role in converting an abstract thought into voluntary action.

blocks.title: Components of the basal ganglia
rows: Functionally related to the basal ganglia but not considered part of the structure

blocks.text: Obsessive-compulsive disorder links to the lentiform nucleus (putamen plus globus pallidus); positron emission tomography shows caudate and lentiform dysfunction. Inferior olivary nucleus, medial temporal lobe, dentate nucleus and red nucleus are the distractors.
The basal ganglia receive crucial inputs from the glutamatergic corticostriatal projection.

blocks.caption: Table: Disorder vs Nature of basal ganglia dysfunction (Obsessive-compulsive disorder, Tourette's syndrome, Huntington chorea, Wilson disease, carbon monoxide poisoning, Hemiballismus, Parkinsonism, Fahr's disease).

blocks.title: Basal ganglia dysfunction in disorders
rows: Volumetric changes and higher blood flow to the caudate nuclei; increased caudate metabolism in untreated subjects reduces after effective treatment
Degeneration of the striatum (mainly caudate nucleus) and selective loss of GABAergic neurons
Copper deposits in the lenticular nuclei
Acute bilateral anoxic damage to basal ganglia
Depigmentation of substantia nigra; Lewy bodies seen; striatal overactivity associated with bradykinesia
Progressive calcium deposition in the basal ganglia (early onset: schizophreniform psychoses and catatonia; later onset: dementia and choreoathetosis)

blocks.text: Huntington disease = degeneration of the striatum (caudate shrinks dramatically; rigidity with superimposed choreiform movements). Subthalamic nucleus is the distractor - its lesion gives hemiballismus instead.
Subthalamic lesion = hemiballismus (flailing ballistic limb movements) - Huntington chorea, dystonia, athetosis and Parkinson disease are the movement-disorder distractors.

blocks.subtopic: Substantia nigra melanin; nucleus accumbens = ventral striatum
blocks.note: **Q23** (keyed substantia nigra): it contains melanin pigment, hence 'black substance'; it has two parts, one functionally equivalent to globus pallidus interna. **Q58** (keyed ventral striatum): nucleus accumbens forms the main part of the ventral striatum. The notes mention only substantia nigra depigmentation in Parkinsonism and nucleus accumbens as reward regulator.

blocks.text: The basal ganglia nucleus with melanin pigment is the substantia nigra (the 'black substance'; one part is functionally equivalent to globus pallidus interna, the other degenerates in Parkinson disease) - not globus pallidus, caudate, subthalamic nuclei or putamen.
Nucleus accumbens forms the main part of the ventral striatum - not hypothalamus, pineal gland, dorsal thalamus or orbitofrontal cortex.

Reward processing = nucleus accumbens. The explanation says amygdala also has a role in stimulus-reward learning, but the nucleus accumbens codes expected positive incentive value, and is the keyed answer.

bullets.text: Basal ganglia: largest subcortical gray matter structure; planning/programming of movement.
Striatum = caudate + putamen; pallidum = globus pallidus; putamen + globus pallidus = lenticular/lentiform nucleus. Subthalamic nuclei and substantia nigra are related but not part.
Glutamatergic corticostriatal input; Alexander's five circuits: motor, oculomotor, dorsolateral prefrontal (executive), anterior cingulate (motivation), lateral orbitofrontal (social intelligence).
Obsessive-compulsive disorder: caudate volume/blood-flow change; Tourette's: striatal dopaminergic dysfunction; Huntington: striatal (caudate) degeneration with loss of GABAergic neurons.

Wilson: copper in lenticular nuclei; carbon monoxide poisoning: bilateral anoxic damage; hemiballismus: subthalamic nucleus damage; Parkinsonism: depigmented substantia nigra, Lewy bodies; Fahr's: calcium deposition.
Obsessive-compulsive disorder: caudate and lentiform nucleus dysfunction on positron emission tomography.
Huntington disease: striatum degeneration (caudate shrinks).
Reward processing = nucleus accumbens (nucleus accumbens codes expected positive incentive value).

blocks.text: The thalamus is a large oval mass of grey matter nuclei in the subcortical region, relaying all types of sensory information onto the cortex (except olfaction). It also relays cerebellar and basal ganglia inputs to the cerebral cortex, and is said to play a crucial role in filtering sensory information in preparation for cortical processing.

blocks.title: Thalamic nuclei mentioned in the notes
rows: Part of the limbic system; receives the mammillothalamic tract and fornix and connects to the cingulate cortex - relays information from hypothalamus and hippocampus onto the frontal cortex

blocks.subtopic: Visual pathway: lateral geniculate body and Meyer's loop
blocks.note: The notes say only that the optic nerve relays via the thalamus (geniculate body). **Q32** (keyed lateral geniculate body): optic radiations run from the lateral geniculate body to the occipital visual cortex. **Q41** (keyed temporal lobe): fibres detouring through the anterior temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) carry the contralateral superior quadrant, so damage gives contralateral homonymous superior quadrantanopsia. Not in the notes.

blocks.text: Visual pathway structure = lateral geniculate body (optic radiations run from it to the occipital visual cortex); medial geniculate body, Heschl's gyrus and inferior colliculus are the auditory-side distractors.

Homonymous **SUPERIOR** quadrantanopsia localises to the temporal lobe (Meyer's loop), not the lateral geniculate body or occipital lobe: fibres detour through the anterior temporal lobe and carry the contralateral superior quadrant.

bullets.text: Thalamus relays all sensory information to cortex except olfaction, plus cerebellar and basal ganglia inputs; filters sensory information.
Anterior thalamus (limbic): receives mammillothalamic tract and fornix, connects to cingulate cortex.
Pulvinar = visual attention; reticular nucleus generates sleep spindles.
Meyer's loop (anterior temporal lobe) lesion = contralateral superior quadrantanopsia.

blocks.text: The hypothalamus regulates physiological functions such as eating, drinking, sleeping and temperature regulation. It has chemoreceptors that respond to variations in glucose levels, osmolarity and acid balance, and plays a major role in neuroendocrine control.

blocks.title: Hypothalamic feeding centres
rows: Satiety centre; in animals, a lesion causes hyperphagia and obesity

blocks.text: The inferior olivary nucleus is located in the brainstem and aids motor coordination by projecting climbing fibers to the contralateral cerebellar cortex via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.

blocks.caption: Boxed text: INFERIOR OLIVARY NUCLEUS - location and function (climbing fibres to the contralateral cerebellar cortex via the inferior cerebellar peduncle), and the effects of inferior olivary lesions as printed.

blocks.title: Cerebellar lesion vs inferior olivary lesion
rows: Ataxia and coarse intentional tremors, hypotonia, past pointing, pendular knee jerk
Appendicular ataxia due to motor incoordination; patients fail the finger-nose test, mimicking a cerebellar lesion

blocks.text: **Q42**: the satiety centre of the hypothalamus is the ventromedial hypothalamus (lateral hypothalamus = feeding centre; ventromedial hypothalamus lesion in animals gives hyperphagia and obesity).

Prolactin regulation: the arcuate nucleus (not suprachiasmatic, preoptic or subthalamic nucleus) holds the prolactin-releasing factor; dopamine via the tuberoinfundibular system regulates prolactin secretion through direct projection to the pituitary.

blocks.subtopic: Hypothalamus in depression
blocks.note: Mock explanation (keyed: hypothalamus): a vignette of depressed mood, anhedonia, initial and terminal insomnia, appetite and weight loss and reduced sexual arousal suggests hypothalamic dysfunction; the explanation says an intrinsic regulatory defect involving the hypothalamus (and monoamine pathways) underlies major depression. Hippocampus, corpus callosum, frontal lobes and pituitary are the distractors. Not in the notes.

bullets.text: Hypothalamus regulates eating, drinking, sleeping, temperature; chemoreceptors for glucose, osmolarity, acid balance; major neuroendocrine role.
Ventromedial hypothalamus = satiety centre (lesion in animals: hyperphagia, obesity); lateral hypothalamus = feeding centre.
Inferior olivary nucleus: brainstem; climbing fibers to contralateral cerebellar cortex via inferior cerebellar peduncle.
Inferior olivary lesion: contralateral appendicular ataxia, fails finger-nose test (mimics cerebellar lesion, which is ipsilateral).
Depression with vegetative features: hypothalamic regulatory defect (not in notes).

blocks.text: The cerebellum prepares a motor plan and predicts the balance needed between muscle groups to carry out the intended action smoothly.

Ataxia with nystagmus and a cerebellar infarct = flocculonodular (vestibular) lobe: loss of equilibrium and a wide-stance gait. The lateral zone (cerebrocerebellum) instead gives hypotonia, dysarthria, dysdiadochokinesia and tremor.

The role of the cerebellum in cognitive processes is increasingly appreciated. Cognitive dysmetria (Andreasen) refers to difficulty in coordinating and monitoring the receiving, processing and expressing of information, which could result from disrupted cortico-cerebellar circuitry in schizophrenia.

blocks.subtopic: Cerebellar damage and dysarthria
blocks.note: **Q30** (keyed cerebellum): extensive cerebellar damage causes 'scanning speech', a dysarthria with poor modulation, irregular cadence and inability to separate adjacent sounds. Not in the notes.

blocks.text: Dysarthria localises to the cerebellum: extensive damage gives 'scanning speech' (poor modulation, irregular cadence, inability to separate adjacent sounds) - homunculus, parietal and temporal lobe, spinal cord are the distractors.

bullets.text: Cerebellum prepares the motor plan and predicts balance between muscle groups.
Lesions: ataxia, coarse intentional tremors, hypotonia, past pointing, pendular knee jerk.
Cognitive dysmetria (Andreasen): disrupted cortico-cerebellar circuitry in schizophrenia.
Flocculonodular lobe damage: loss of equilibrium and wide-based gait.

blocks.text: The brain stem is made of the midbrain, pons and medulla. Most of the cranial nerves (9 out of 12) enter or exit the brain from the brainstem.

blocks.title: Brain stem divisions
rows: Superior colliculi (conjugate gaze control) and inferior colliculi (auditory source localization); substantia nigra; periaqueductal grey matter (vocalization, freezing response to threat, pain suppression)
Positioned beneath the cerebellum; surrounds the upper half of the 4th ventricle
Surrounds the inferior part of the 4th ventricle; continuous with the spinal cord

blocks.caption: Table (page 5): Cranial nerves, columns No. / Name / Anatomical features, rows I Olfactory to VI Abducens.
Table (page 6, continued): Cranial nerves, rows VII Facial, VIII Vestibular, Cochlear, IX Glossopharyngeal, X Vagus, XI Accessory, XII Hypoglossal, with their anatomical features as printed.

blocks.title: Cranial nerves I-XII
rows: Runs on the basal surface of frontal cortex without passing through the thalamus; outgrowth of forebrain
Also an outgrowth of the forebrain; relays via thalamus (geniculate body)
Purely motor; supplies four of the six ocular muscles
Purely motor; supplies superior oblique (ocular muscle)
Both sensory and motor; transmits facial sensation, controls jaw muscles
Purely motor; supplies the lateral rectus (ocular muscle). The source notes print 'lateral abducens', which is a typo; the **Q18** explanation confirms lateral rectus.
Both sensory and motor; transmits taste sensation, controls facial muscles

Vestibular division transmits balance sensation; cochlear division transmits auditory (hearing) sensation. Reviewer correction (not in the source): the source notes (page 6) print these the other way round (vestibular = auditory, cochlear = balance), which is a typo.
Motor control of pharynx; parasympathetic control of parotid gland; taste from back of tongue
Motor control of larynx and pharynx; parasympathetic control of viscera; visceral sensations

blocks.text: Purely motor cranial nerve (of the options): abducens - each option set offers only **ONE** of the three purely motor nerves (**III**, **IV**, **VI**) beside sensory/mixed ones (vestibulocochlear, glossopharyngeal, olfactory, optic). Abducens impairment gives inward deviation with no ptosis or pupil change.

Same question, different option set: here oculomotor (**III**) is the only purely motor nerve (facial, vagus, glossopharyngeal, vestibulocochlear are mixed or sensory). Its impairment gives dilated pupil, ptosis and outward deviation, and impairs the efferent limb of the light and accommodation reflexes.
Loss of taste from the anterior tongue = 7th (facial) nerve palsy via the chorda tympani, which crosses the middle ear and can be damaged by severe infection - not 5th, 6th, 8th or 9th.
Olfactory is the only cranial nerve without a thalamic relay (the notes say the optic nerve relays via the thalamus) - trigeminal, optic, abducens and oculomotor are the distractors.

blocks.subtopic: Structure spared in normal ageing
blocks.note: Mock explanation (keyed: cranial nerve nuclei): cranial nerve nuclei are spared during normal ageing; cerebellum, motor neurons, cerebral cortex and subthalamic nuclei could all be affected. Not in the notes.

blocks.subtopic: Cranial nerve VIII: typo in the source notes
blocks.note: The source notes (page 6) print 'Vestibular - transmits auditory sensation' and 'Cochlear - transmits balance sensation'. This is a typo in the notes. Reviewer correction (not in the source): the correct attribution, used in the table above, is vestibular = balance, cochlear = hearing. Learn the correct version. (**Q18** does not settle it: it lists 'Vestibulocochlear' as a nerve with sensory function.)

blocks.mnemonic: Oh Oh Oh To Touch And Feel Very Good Velvet, Ah Heaven

blocks.subtopic: Midbrain structures from embryology questions
blocks.note: **Q61** (keyed red nucleus): the mesencephalon (midbrain) includes the red nucleus. **Q60**: the ventral tegmental area is in the midbrain. Neither the red nucleus nor the ventral tegmental area's midbrain location is stated in the notes' brain stem paragraph.

blocks.text: Constituent of the mesencephalon = red nucleus; the subthalamus (diencephalon) and cerebellum (metencephalon, with the pons) are distractors from other embryonic divisions; the explanation places the red nucleus in the midbrain.

bullets.text: Brain stem = midbrain, pons, medulla; 9 of 12 cranial nerves attach to it.
Midbrain: superior colliculi (gaze), inferior colliculi (auditory localisation), substantia nigra, periaqueductal grey (vocalization, freezing, pain suppression).
Pons lies beneath cerebellum, around upper 4th ventricle; medulla around lower 4th ventricle, continuous with spinal cord.

I (olfactory) runs on the basal frontal surface and does not pass through the thalamus; I and II (optic) are both outgrowths of the forebrain; II relays via the thalamus (geniculate body). VIII: vestibular division = balance, cochlear division = hearing (reviewer correction, not in the source: the notes print these reversed).
Purely motor: III (four of six ocular muscles), IV (superior oblique), VI (lateral ocular muscle). Mixed: V (face sensation, jaw), VII (taste, facial muscles).
IX: pharynx motor, parotid parasympathetic, posterior tongue taste. X: larynx/pharynx motor, visceral parasympathetic and sensation. XI: neck muscles. XII: tongue muscles.
Oculomotor palsy: dilated pupil, ptosis, outward deviation.
Olfactory nerve is the only cranial nerve with no thalamic relay.
Cranial nerve nuclei are spared in normal ageing (not in notes).

bullets.text: Bilateral anterior cerebral artery infarct: quadriparesis (legs weaker than arms) and akinetic mutism.

Anterior cerebral artery occlusion: contralateral leg weakness; bilateral: gait apraxia and incontinence.

blocks.text: Frontal-to-frontal communication runs through the **GENU** of the corpus callosum (the splenium is the tempting distractor, as are fornix, parahippocampal gyrus and arcuate fasciculus).

The pericallosal artery, derived from the anterior cerebral artery, supplies the anterior aspect and most of the body of the corpus callosum. Left-sided apraxia and agnosia may be seen with vascular disruption.

The posterior cerebral artery territory supplies the splenium (posterior corpus callosum); disrupted supply prevents the right visual cortex accessing dominant-hemisphere processes such as language, resulting in alexia and colour anomia, with preserved ability to copy words because motor information is relayed via the anterior corpus callosum.

blocks.title: Named tracts
rows: Connects hippocampus to hypothalamus via mammillary bodies; relays cortical input to regulate neuroendocrine and autonomic systems
Major frontotemporal tract connecting orbitofrontal cortex to the anterior temporal lobes; important in social cognition and language

blocks.text: The tract linking Wernicke's and Broca's areas is the arcuate fasciculus (dominant hemisphere); anterior and habenular commissures, cingulate gyrus and planum temporale are the distractors. Dominant arcuate lesions can cause conduction aphasia.

**Q14**: the artery supplying most of the corpus callosum is the anterior cerebral artery (rich supply from anterior cerebral and anterior communicating, also posterior cerebral; bilateral anterior cerebral artery occlusion infarcts both frontal lobes and the anterior corpus callosum).

bullets.text: Projection fibers vertical (higher-lower); association fibers within a hemisphere; commissural fibers between hemispheres.
Corpus callosum = largest commissure; others: anterior (olfactory bulbs), posterior (pretectal nuclei), hippocampal, habenular (posterior dorsal thalamic nuclei).
Pericallosal artery (from anterior cerebral artery) supplies anterior and most of the body of the corpus callosum; disruption: left-sided apraxia and agnosia.
Posterior cerebral artery supplies the splenium; disruption: alexia and colour anomia with preserved word copying.

Fornix: hippocampus to hypothalamus via mammillary bodies. Arcuate fasciculus: Broca-Wernicke, damage = conduction aphasia. Uncinate fasciculus: orbitofrontal cortex to anterior temporal lobe, social cognition and language.
Genu of corpus callosum links the two frontal lobes.
Arcuate fasciculus (dominant hemisphere) links Wernicke and Broca areas; lesion = conduction aphasia.

blocks.text: The human brain contains approximately 10^11 neurons and approximately 10^12 glial cells (printed '1011' and '1012' in the notes; the superscript exponents appear to have lost their formatting). Brodmann divided the cortex into 47 'specialised' areas according to the distribution of neuron types (cytoarchitecture).

The neocortex (most of the cerebrum) has six layers, with the pial surface above layer 1 and white matter below layer 6. Layers 2 and 4 are mainly afferent (receiving inputs); layers 5 and 6 are mainly efferent (sending outputs).
Pyramidal neurons, with triangular cell bodies, make up nearly ==75%== of cortical neurons. Stellate cells (==25%==) are present in all layers except layer 1.

Layer 4 (internal granular) receives thalamocortical input; layer 5 holds the largest pyramidal cells (Betz cells in motor cortex); layer 6 (multiform) is the main source of corticothalamic fibres.

Layer **IV** of the cerebral cortex (from thalamus feeding forward to pyramidal cells) and also the cerebellum

blocks.text: Neuron with **NO** axon = amacrine neuron; Golgi type 1 has a long axon and Golgi type 2 a short axon ending near the parent cell.

bullets.text: Purkinje cells: GABAergic, cerebellar cortex only, sole output of cerebellar motor coordination (inhibitory to deep nuclei).
Granule cells: cerebellar granular layer, cortical layer 4, hippocampal dentate gyrus, olfactory bulb.
Betz cells: large pyramidal cells in layer 5 of primary motor cortex; largest central nervous system neurons (up to 100 micrometres); ~10% of layer V pyramidal cells.
Stellate cells: layer IV of cerebral cortex (thalamus to pyramidal cells) and cerebellum.
Purkinje cells are found only in the cerebellar cortex (GABAergic, sole output).
Golgi type 1 = long axon; type 2 = short axon; amacrine = no axon.

facts.label: Betz cells share of layer V pyramidal cells

blocks.text: Glial cells have supportive metabolic functions and also modulate neuronal function, e.g. via production of neurosteroids. The notes say there are 3 types but go on to list four (astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, and ependymal cells described as 'a special type of glia').

blocks.title: Glial cells
rows: Most numerous; star-shaped; enable nutrition of neurons, break down some neurotransmitters, maintain the blood-brain barrier
Seen in the central nervous system (replaced by Schwann cells in peripheral nerves); produce myelin sheaths that help saltatory conduction and quicken signal transmission
Descendants of macrophages; scavenger cells that clear neuronal debris following cell death
Cover the ventricles and facilitate cerebrospinal fluid circulation via their ciliary processes

blocks.text: **NOT** an astrocyte function: forming the central nervous system myelin sheath (that is the oligodendrocyte). Astrocytes nourish neurons, deactivate some neurotransmitters and contribute to the blood-brain barrier.

blocks.text: Microglia statement that is correct = mesodermal origin (so they share features with myeloid cells); the distractors (myelination, ==70%== of glia, sodium-channel sensitivity, present outside brain and spinal cord) are all wrong.

items.text: Descendants of macrophages clearing neuronal debris = microglial cells.
Schwann cells are the neuroglia of the peripheral nervous system (oligodendrocytes do this in the central nervous system).
Myelination is the oligodendrocyte function - not metabolic transmitter clearance, gliosis, structural support or blood-brain barrier contribution.

Scavenger cells at central nervous system injury sites = microglia (ependymal cells aid cerebrospinal fluid flow; Schwann cells form peripheral nervous system myelin; satellite cells support ganglion neurons).
Macrophages of the central nervous system = microglia (non-neuronal, mesoderm-derived).
Ependymal cells line the ventricular walls and enable cerebrospinal fluid circulation.
Glutamate dehydrogenase is seen only in astrocytes - catechol-O-methyltransferase, monoamine oxidase B, tyrosine hydroxylase and acetylcholinesterase are the distractors.
Regulating extracellular potassium around neuronal cell bodies = astrocytes (they also insulate and separate neurons).

bullets.text: Glia: supportive and metabolic; modulate neurons (e.g. neurosteroids).
Astrocytes: most numerous, star-shaped; neuronal nutrition, breakdown of some neurotransmitters, blood-brain barrier.
Oligodendrocytes: central nervous system myelin (Schwann cells in peripheral nervous system); saltatory conduction.
Microglia: macrophage descendants, scavenge neuronal debris. Ependymal cells: line ventricles, ciliary action aids cerebrospinal fluid circulation.
Central nervous system myelination is an oligodendrocyte, not astrocyte, function.

blocks.text: The blood-brain barrier is located in the endothelial cells of brain capillaries. Unlike endothelial cells elsewhere, brain endothelial cells have tight junctions with high electrical resistance, providing an effective barrier against molecules. Brain capillaries are also in contact with foot processes of astrocytes that separate the capillaries from the neurons.

blocks.title: What crosses the barrier
rows: Penetrate relatively easily via the lipid membranes of the cells
Unable to cross without specialised carrier-mediated transport mechanisms

blocks.text: Inflammation such as meningitis weakens the blood-brain barrier.

blocks.subtopic: Anterior pituitary has a blood-brain barrier
blocks.note: Mock explanation (keyed: anterior pituitary is the area that does **NOT** lack the barrier): circumventricular organs such as subfornical organ, area postrema (chemoreceptor trigger zone), median eminence and posterior pituitary lack it, with fenestrated capillaries as in peripheral tissue. Keep the contrast: anterior pituitary has the barrier, posterior pituitary does not.

blocks.text: **Q40**: lipophilic substances penetrate the barrier better; endothelial cells are joined by tight junctions (not gap junctions); inflammation weakens (not strengthens) the barrier; the barrier is formed by endothelial cells, not microglial foot processes; the basal forebrain is not named as lacking the barrier.

bullets.text: Blood-brain barrier sits in brain capillary endothelial cells with tight junctions of high electrical resistance, plus astrocyte foot processes.
Lipid-soluble molecules (ethanol, caffeine) cross easily; water-soluble ions (sodium, potassium) need carrier-mediated transport.
Inflammation (meningitis) weakens the barrier.
No barrier at circumventricular organs: subfornical organ, area postrema, median eminence, posterior pituitary.
Anterior pituitary has the barrier; posterior pituitary, median eminence, area postrema, subfornical organ lack it.

blocks.title: Dopaminergic pathways by length

Blockade produces the desirable antipsychotic effect by controlling positive psychotic symptoms
Ventral tegmental area to cingulate cortex and prefrontal regions via medial forebrain bundle

blocks.text: Ventral tegmental area location = midbrain (medial to the substantia nigra), origin of the mesocorticolimbic system - not pons, medulla, occipital or temporal lobe.

Addictive behaviour involves the ventral tegmental area, nucleus accumbens and septal nucleus (dopamine in ventral tegmental area and nucleus accumbens); suprachiasmatic nucleus, nucleus tractus solitarius, substantia nigra and preoptic nucleus are the distractors.

bullets.text: Long paths: nigrostriatal, mesocortical, mesolimbic; short: tuberoinfundibular, incertohypothalamic; ultrashort: retinal amacrine cells and olfactory system.
Nigrostriatal (substantia nigra to striatum): motor control, most brain dopamine; dopamine deficiency/blockade causes extrapyramidal effects.
Mesolimbic (ventral tegmental area to nucleus accumbens/hippocampus): blockade = antipsychotic effect on positive symptoms.
Mesocortical (ventral tegmental area to cingulate/prefrontal): low dopamine or blockade = negative symptoms.
Tuberoinfundibular: dopamine is prolactin inhibitory hormone, blockade raises prolactin; incertohypothalamic: thermoregulation, possibly weight gain.
Addiction circuitry: ventral tegmental area, nucleus accumbens, septal nucleus (dopaminergic).

blocks.title: Cholinergic pathways
rows: Innervates thalamic relay neurons and reticular nuclei; part of the ascending reticular activating system, important to maintain wakefulness and rapid eye movement sleep
Projects to hippocampus, frontal cortex and amygdala; degeneration implicated in Alzheimer's disease

blocks.text: Most of the brain's serotonergic neurons originate in the midbrain dorsal and median raphe nuclei and ascend to innervate the entire cortex, basal ganglia and thalamus, and also descend to the spinal cord.

The noradrenergic projection originates at the locus coeruleus (pons) and ascends to most of the cortex via the medial forebrain bundle; like the serotonin system, it also descends to the spinal cord.

bullets.text: Cholinergic brainstem pathway (pedunculopontine, laterodorsal tegmental nuclei) = part of the ascending reticular activating system: wakefulness and rapid eye movement sleep.
Cholinergic basal forebrain pathway: nucleus basalis of Meynert to hippocampus, frontal cortex, amygdala; degenerates in Alzheimer's.
Serotonin: dorsal and median raphe nuclei (midbrain) to cortex, basal ganglia, thalamus and spinal cord.
Noradrenaline: locus coeruleus (pons) to most of the cortex via medial forebrain bundle, and to the spinal cord.

blocks.text: Glutamate is the most common excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain, so almost all cortical descending tracts (from pyramidal cells) use it; this large corticofugal output makes up most of the corona radiata. All association and commissural fibres are glutamatergic, as are many thalamic neurons (so thalamocortical projections too).
Cerebellar output from deep nuclei, subthalamic nuclei to globus pallidus projections, and brainstem-to-spinal cord projections are also predominantly glutamatergic.

Gamma-aminobutyric acid is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain. Unlike other transmitters, there are no specific neurochemical pathways where GABA dominates; it is the major transmitter of cerebral interneurons, which are ubiquitous throughout the cortex.
Interneurons are usually short neurons connecting two other neurons; they carry neither motor nor sensory information but modulate local neural circuitry.

blocks.title: Cortical GABAergic interneuron subtypes
rows: About ==40%== of all interneurons; reduced frontal cortex expression is a well-replicated feature of schizophrenia; two subtypes: basket cells and chandelier cells
==30%== of interneurons; also called Martinotti cells
Receive direct thalamocortical input; synapse with soma or dendrites of pyramidal neurons; provide excitatory-inhibitory balance
Synapse with the proximal axonal hillock of pyramidal neurons; may have an overall excitatory role by short-circuiting action potential propagation, though the role is still unclear

bullets.text: Glutamate = most common excitatory transmitter: cortical descending tracts (most of corona radiata), association and commissural fibres, many thalamic neurons (thalamocortical).
Also glutamatergic: cerebellar deep-nuclei output, subthalamic nuclei to globus pallidus, brainstem to spinal cord.
Gamma-aminobutyric acid = primary inhibitory transmitter; no dominant GABA pathway - major transmitter of cortical interneurons.
Two cortical interneuron subtypes: parvalbumin (~40%) and somatostatin (30%, Martinotti cells).

Parvalbumin interneuron reduction in frontal cortex is a replicated finding in schizophrenia; parvalbumin types: basket cells (thalamocortical input, excitatory-inhibitory balance) and chandelier cells (axonal hillock).

Left-handers: bank explanation gives 67% left-hemisphere language dominance (notes: 64%).
